clinical_targets.goal: Complete Response (CR) or Partial Response (PR) / Stable Disease (SD)
Prolongation of survival with preserved ECOG performance status 0–1
Maintain treatment-related toxicities at Grade 1 or lower

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Uterine Cancer focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Uterine Cancer.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Uterine Cancer.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Uterine Cancer require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Uterine Cancer.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose reduction or hydration protocols required for nephrotoxic antineoplastics (cisplatin, methotrexate).
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor total bilirubin, transaminases, and alkaline phosphatase before each chemotherapy cycle.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Chemotherapy contraindicated in first trimester; multidisciplinary tumor board consultation required.
special_populations.elderly: Comprehensive geriatric assessment to balance treatment efficacy against myelosuppression and cardiac toxicity.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is uterine cancer? Uterine cancer is a cancer that forms in tissues of the uterus , which is sometimes called the womb. The uterus is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. There are two types of uterine cancer: Endometrial cancer is the most common type. This type of cancer begins in the cells lining the uterus, known as the endometrium. Uterine sarcoma is a rare, more aggressive cancer that is harder to treat. This type of cancer begins in muscle or other tissues in the uterus. Who is more likely to develop uterine cancer? Uterine cancer usually happens after menopause. The cause is unknown. However, some factors and conditions that change the balance of hormones in your body may increase your risk. These can include obesity or metabolic syndrome (a group of risk factors for certain health problems). Other factors and conditions that may increase your risk for: Endometrial cancer Taking estrogen-only hormone therapy after menopause. Having type 2 diabetes Starting menstruation at an early age or menopause at a later age Having never been pregnant Taking tamoxifen, a medicine used to prevent or treat breast cancer Having polycystic ovary syndrome Having a mother, sister, or daughter who has had endometrial cancer Having certain genetic conditions, such as Lynch syndrome Having endometrial hyperplasia (thickening of the uterine lining) Uterine sarcoma Having had past treatment with radiation therapy to the pelvis Taking tamoxifen, a medicine used to prevent or treat breast cancer What are the symptoms of uterine cancer? The most common symptom of both endometrial cancer and uterine sarcoma is abnormal vaginal bleeding . Both types of uterine cancer may also cause pelvic pain or pressure, unusual vaginal discharge, or an enlarged uterus or pelvic mass. Less common symptoms may include urinating (peeing) often, having trouble urinating, or pain during sexual intercourse. How is uterine cancer diagnosed? If you have symptoms of uterine cancer, your health care provider may: Ask about your medical history and family health history Do a pelvic exam Order imaging tests Suggest a biopsy or a minor procedure called dilation and curettage (D & C) to check the lining of your uterus What are the treatments for uterine cancer? Treatment may depend on your health, how much cancer you have, and whether it has spread. The most common treatment is having a hysterectomy , which is surgery to remove the uterus. Sometimes the surgery also removes the ovaries and fallopian tubes. You may have more than one type of treatment. Other treatments may include: Hormone therapy Radiation therapy Chemotherapy Can uterine cancer be prevented? There is no sure way to prevent uterine cancer. But you can do things that may help lower your risk such as aiming for a healthy weight , getting regular physical activity , and talking to your provider about the benefits and risks of hormone therapy. NIH: National Cancer Institute
style_3_monograph.treatment: After you are diagnosed, a careful history and exam will be done to make sure the cancer has not spread to other organs. Chemotherapy is the main type of treatment. It is usually effective. A hysterectomy to remove the womb and radiation treatment are rarely needed.
